title.value: Which role does the lienear component actually play

comment.value:
Dear authors,
thank you very much for your extensive answer and the new experiments provided. I acknowledge that you have invested considerable effort to facilitate an open discussion. 

Theory: Your statement that the Lipsjitz property follows from continuity on a compact set in Theorem 1 is obviously wrong - take the sqrt on [0,1] as an example.  But uniform continuity should do to complete your argument. Lemma 9 seems to contain the implicit assumption that M<=N, otherwise your projection method won't work.

It turns out that the expressivity of your networks is mostly due to the expressivity of the transformations g_y,g_x and the linear piece A only plays the minor role of not messing this up, i.e. keeping the input points separated. 

In fact, in the view of the strong results of universal approximation of orientation preserving diffeomeorphisms by Techima and the Brenier-Gangbo theorem that diffeomorphisms are dense in L^p acually much stronger UAP-results can be obtaines, e.g. if you choose g__y=id and A in some trivial way (like a projection to R^N). E.g. distributional UAP immediataly follows from this (with a little bit of transport theory) So it is hard to me to attribute these facts to the linear structure which has the main role to stay out of the way.

Experiments: Thank you fro clarifying that A g_x and g_y are trained jointly. But like in my comments conscerning the theory, you don't really to set up your training on the basis of the linear structure and my suspicion is that the affine coupling layers in g_x and g_y do most of the work and linear solves don't. 

Thank you for the new experiments. I interpret these experiments that (with a few exceptions like with BetaH) you obtain marginal positive effects with a certain reliability, which is fine but not really convincing on the ICLR level. 

I acknowledge that the improved documentation of the implementation and the additional visuals helped the paper.

I'm still not happy - agreeing with another referee - that instead of performing numerous detailed computations the transport of structure should be emphasized which would shorten the mathematical argument considerably. Given this viewpoint, your results are pretty evident.

In conclusion, I am not inclined to improve my score. Mainly, because the nonlinear parts of your architecture seem to do most of the work and the linear stuff has mostly seems to have the role of not getting into the way and maybe help here and there a little bit, both in theory and experiment. This is not what i expect from the bold title.

summary.value:
The paper proposes to use invertible neural networks as non linear coordinate transformations of vector spaces R^n and to consider the linear structure within one such coordinate representation, leading to a non classical linear structure in the other and to a non-linear structure w.r.t. the standard operations on R^n. The authors thereafter consider the linear operations with respect to the deformed addition and scalar multiiplication. When seeing the results from the angle of non linear coordinates of a vector space, the results of the given Lemma are pretty straight forward, but valuable for less mathematically oriented readers. 
Interestingly, the authors can then employ their linearization approach in learning image synthesis style transfer. The FM generation paths that usually require the solution of a non linear ODE can, in the linearized representation be represented by a learned linear map that is obtained as the time integral of a linear vector field A_t v which is represented by a neural network. When the solution operator to A_t is computed once, this can be used for a essentially lossless one step generation.
The authors demonstrate the viability of their approach for MNIST and Celebrity Faces image generation tasks and neural style transfer. The results are decent and show the potential of the author's point of view.

strengths.value:
* the paper provides a really original idea to consider invertible neural networks in vector spaces and then build machine learning tasks on linear methods in the constructed latent space
* The authors show that this approach can be combined with generative learning tasks in the image domain, in particular that the time integration of the FM vector field can be effectively represented by a linear solution operator obtained as the time integration of (time dependent) linear vector fields.
* The theoretical documentation is rather complete and easy to follow

weaknesses.value:
- The core idea of the paper - looking at vector spaces in non linear coordinates - could be presented somewhat clearer. Many results given in the lemma would then just be clear and in parts superfluous (like Lemma 4). Also all the linear algebra checked in detail would follow from one structural argument. 
- Better visualizations would be really helpful for a better representation of the main idea. 
- For me the missing part is a detailed investigation of the interaction of the chosen 'coordinate maps' g with the learning task. Obviously not any g would do (e.g. not the identity or linear g's).
- Related to this, I would appreciate a much more extensive analysis of the training details, especially with regard to the previous point.
- Also the interaction between the learning task and the expressivity of the linearizers would be of interest. Is the reproduction of the FM time integration with a linear flow compatible with other approaches that do not have as 'stiff' vector fields as FM - take e.g. a likelihood based trained neuralODE. Similar questions arise for the style transfer task.
- The title, due to its generality, somehow promises more than is kept by the rather specific application domain.
- The authors address flow matching as diffusion. As an ODE based method it is not a diffusion process, unlike SDE based DDPM. In a mathematically based paper, such inaccuracies should be avoided.

Dear Reviewer ojRH,

As the discussion period advances, we wanted to gently ensure you had a chance to see our updates, which directly address the specific requests in your review:

- **Visuals:** We added Figure 10 (Appendix I) to visualize the geometric intuition of the induced space.

- **Implementation:** We added a summary table in Section 2 and expanded Appendix G with reproducible details on training the coordinate maps.

- **Theory:** We added the Finite Dataset Approximation Theorem (Appendix H) to formally establish the expressivity of the framework.

- **Experiments:** We added three diverse tasks (Weather Forecasting, CelebA Classification, Disentanglement) to demonstrate viability beyond toy generation.

We remain available for any further discussion and would be happy to provide additional clarifications or improvements if needed. Your comments were valuable and we are open to any further suggestions.

# Do we have any universal approximation results (or approximation results in some restricted class of functions or families of functions) for the linearizers?

Thank you for this excellent question. It motivated us to formalize an important theoretical guarantee. Yes, thanks to you, we have now proven that **Linearizers can approximate any function arbitrarily well on finite datasets** (the practical setting we always train in). 


**Finite Dataset Approximation Theorem (Appendix H):** Let $\mathcal{X} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$ 
be a finite dataset and $F: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^M$ be any target function. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist 
invertible neural networks $G_x, G_y$ and a linear map $A$ such that the Linearizer 
$\hat{F}(x) := G_y^{-1}(A G_x(x))$ achieves $\sup_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \|\hat{F}(x) - F(x)\| < \varepsilon$.

**Proof sketch:** (1) By standard results in differential topology, diffeomorphisms 
can map any finite set of distinct points to any other finite set. (2) We construct 
an ideal Linearizer $ F^* $ that perfectly fits the data by mapping data points to simple 
latent coordinates (e.g., $p_i = (i,0,\ldots,0)$), applying a simple linear map, and mapping 
outputs back to targets. (3) Since INNs can approximate any diffeomorphism arbitrarily 
well on compact sets (Teshima et al., 2020), our INN-based Linearizer can approximate 
$F^*$ to arbitrary accuracy. The complete formal proof with $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ analysis is in Appendix H.

This establishes universal approximation on finite datasets (the practical training setting). This theoretical result suggests that with enough parameters a Linearizer can fit any dataset. We do point to two limitations. The first is that this theorem is for **finite datasets**, not universal approximation over continuous function spaces. The topological constraints discussed in Section 4.1 remain for the global function, but so does the claim about practically fitting subsets. Second, while this result shows expressivity it does not cover optimization that is known to be challenging for architectures with INNs.

 

# In general, please explain in more detail what functions in the linearizer are trained. For example, if you consider one function from $X$ to $Y$, do you find all the maps $g_x$, $g_y$, and the linear operator $A$ by training?

The entire architecture, $f(x) = g_y^{-1}(Ag_x(x))$, is trained end-to-end. The maps $g_x$, $g_y$, and the linear operator $A$ are all learnable and are simultaneously optimized within a regular network training procedure, using the standard loss function for the desired task.

 


# How is training done when you have a family of functions between the same spaces \(X\) and \(Y\)?
For families of functions, which are families of $A$'s applied using the same $g_x,g_y$, we use **Parameterization**. $A$ is parameterized using a hypernetwork, with a condition as input. The parameterization architecture is specified in Appendix G.3. In the flow-matching application this $A_t$ is conditioned on the time-step $t$, whereas the style-transfer is conditioned on a style indicator.

 



# In formula (15), what are the properties of the function \(f(x,t)\)?
$f(x,t) = g^{-1}(A_tg(\cdot))$ is a Linearizer, with the core operator $A_t$ parameterized by $t$ as explained above.

This discussion is not going to be very productive if the authors keep mischaracterizing what I said. I have not said that the collapsing step is trivial because a zero function also collapses steps. That example illustrates that it is not hard to get the collapsing property if one chooses a model with only this property in mind. The greater challenge is to (approximately) collapse steps for the diffusion models that are actually used in practice. The authors keep trying to sell their result for the later. 

Concerning peer review: I somewhat agree here, but I would add that the purpose of peer-reviewing is _not_ to replace proofreading. It is usually expected to provide the best possible version to the reviewers.

# "The experiments are limited to generation tasks on relatively small image datasets, such as MNIST and CelebA. Therefore, their significance is limited from the perspective of practical usefulness."

We acknowledge that the current experimental section does not guarantee success on a large scale. This paper establishes the methodological foundation. We demonstrate breadth across domains rather than depth on one benchmark. Each application shows the framework enables something previously difficult or impossible.

As we state at the beginning of Section 3: " ...we now present proof-of-concept applications that highlight advantages of our framework, leaving scaling and engineering refinements for future work." 

Competing with state-of-the-art on any single task requires extensive, task-specific engineering, compute, and tuning, which was not the goal of this foundational paper. We believe future work can now build on our framework to focus on scaling these specific applications.

 

# "I would like more clarification on the benefit of reframing deep learning models as linear mappings in curved spaces. If all neural networks could be interpreted this way, it would be convincing. However, as this paper itself points out, this is not the case. Therefore, it seems more reasonable to view this paper as proposing a specific type of architecture that combines invertible networks with linear mappings."


It is true that the way to identify the vector spaces over which a mapping is linear is through this specific, learned structure. The benefits of this are numerous, as all the applications and analysis shown in this paper rely on this induced linearity. These include:
- Closure, which allows collapsing entire generative sequences (like the hundreds of sampling steps in flow matching) into a single, equivalent step.
- The ability to derive an analytic Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverse for tasks like generative model inversion.
- Ability to enforce properties like perfect idempotency ($f(f(x))=f(x)$) by architecture.

As noted in the response to the expressive power concern above, the method is applicable practically to any mapping. It does require training or retraining over data, or by distillation. Having the possibility to train for any arbitrary practical task, the range of possibilities is significant and opens the door to use these linear benefits for many other tasks.

- **New Experiments:** We added Weather Forecasting, CelebA Classification, and Disentanglement (Appendix E.3) to demonstrate broad applicability of the Linearizer.

- **Space & Topology:** We clarified that the "Space" is a finite-dimensional vector space equipped with a learned induced inner product topology.

# "The title, due to its generality, somehow promises more than is kept by the rather specific application domain."

Fair point. We appreciate this perspective and acknowledge the title is provocative. However, we would like to point out that the Linearizer is not limited to a specific application domain. We support this claim with three points of evidence, two of which are new as for this rebuttal:
## 1. Feasibility: Intuition regarding the feasibility, that we present in Sec. 4.1 in the paper.
As we argue in Sec. 4.1, the framework's practical expressivity is not really limited in practice. The key insight is that most high-dimensional data (e.g., images, text tokens) resides on a low-dimensional manifold or a small subset of the ambient vector space. This provides the mapping with a large degree of freedom, as it only needs to be well-behaved on this small subset of the ambient vector space.

## 2. Theoretical Guarantee: A new formal proof showing that a Linearizer can fit any finite dataset.
We have added **appendix H**, which presents a finite-dataset universal approximation theorem and formally proves it. This establishes the ability of our architecture, given enough parameters, to fit any finite dataset with arbitrary accuracy.

**Finite Dataset Approximation Theorem (Appendix H):** Let $\mathcal{X} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$ 
be a finite dataset and $F: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^M$ be any target function. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist 
invertible neural networks $G_x, G_y$ and a linear map $A$ such that the Linearizer

**Proof sketch:** (1) By standard results in differential topology, diffeomorphisms

an ideal Linearizer $ F^* $ that perfectly fits the data by mapping data points to simple 
latent coordinates (e.g., $p_i = (i,0,\ldots,0)$), applying a simple linear map, and mapping 
outputs back to targets. (3) Since INNs can approximate any diffeomorphism arbitrarily 
well on compact sets (Teshima et al., 2020), our INN-based Linearizer can approximate 
$F^*$ to arbitrary accuracy. The complete formal proof with $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ analysis is in Appendix H.

I would like to acknowledge that the authors have responded to the questions raised in my previous review. It partly answered my questions.

Based on your response, I have two follow-up comments regarding the assertions made in the manuscript:

1. The statement regarding the set $X$ needs correction. In the statement of the theorem, $X$ is defined as a compact set. However, the proof provided is actually valid only for a finite set. Therefore, the statement must be revised to accurately reflect that the result is proven for finite sets, rather than for general compact sets.

2. The theorem does not hold in dimension 1. For instance, given three points 0, 1, 2 on a 1-dimensional line, it is topologically impossible to map them to 0, 2, 1 respectively via a diffeomorphism. This is because the preservation of order on the real line prevents such a rearrangement without jumping over points. However, I think this is an exceptional case that we can omit from the statement.
Thanks for the reply. The authors have provided answers to my questions. I think the result is a meaningful and relevant contribution to the ML community and maintain my score.

## 3. Empirical Validation: Three new diverse experiments, empirically showing a linearizer converging over various tasks.
While optimizing invertible networks can be challenging, we empirically found that a **Linearizer** can be trained effectively for the tasks we attempted. To address this concern more directly, we broadened our experimental scope with **three** additional and diverse tasks - face attribute classification, disentanglement distillation, and weather prediction - highlighting the robustness of the Linearizer.

**CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA).** We evaluate on the CelebA face attribute classification task, which includes large pose variation, background clutter, diverse identities, and rich annotations (40 binary attributes such as *Male*, *Eyeglasses*, *Blond Hair*). After training, our Linearizer attains a test accuracy of **87.6%**; for reference, a ResNet-50 baseline reaches **86.1%**. These results suggest that the Linearizer handles moderately complex, real-world visual variability.

**Distillation of nonlinear disentanglement models.** Broadening the scope of experimentation, we distill the encoder of a pretrained disentanglement model into a Linearizer (using pretrained checkpoints from [1]). We consider VAE, FactorVAE, and β-VAE on the **dSprites** dataset, which provides ground-truth factors of variation. We assess quality with standard metrics: **FactorVAE**, **SAP**, and **DCI** (disentanglement, completeness, informativeness). Across models, the Linearizer closely matches the original encoders (marked as Linearizer-) on these metrics (see table below), indicating that it can capture highly nonlinear transformations with no loss in disentanglement quality of the encoded representations.

| Model                  | FactorVAE  ↑      | SAP     ↑         | DCI-D    ↑        | DCI-C      ↑      | DCI-I     ↑       |
|------------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| VAE                    | 0.2831±0.0306    | 0.0248±0.0075    | 0.4897±0.0209    | 0.2727±0.0067    | 0.9373±0.0025    |
| Linearizer-VAE         | 0.2875±0.0345    | 0.0232±0.0017    | 0.4945±0.0124    | 0.2704±0.0060    | 0.9348±0.0072    |
| FactorVAE              | 0.3314±0.0135    | 0.0585±0.0086    | 0.6417±0.0120    | 0.5062±0.0051    | 0.9359±0.0035    |
| Linearizer-FactorVAE   | 0.3546±0.0251    | 0.0488±0.0095    | 0.6437±0.0057    | 0.5049±0.0034    | 0.9357±0.0030    |
| BetaH                  | 0.5927±0.0465    | 0.2321±0.0115    | 0.8260±0.0222    | 0.7133±0.0035    | 0.9533±0.0018    |
| Linearizer-BetaH       | 0.6916±0.0496    | 0.2443±0.0083    | 0.7951±0.0038    | 0.7105±0.0038    | 0.9548±0.0010    |



**Weather Prediction.** To further explore the applicability of our framework, we conduct a small experiment in a new domain, regression of future steps. We utilize a standard weather prediction benchmarking, in this benchmark, we need to predict the future, given 96 steps of the past. We compare our method with two well known baselines, the AutoFormer[3] and PatchTST[2], sutied specifically for regression task. Briefly, while our method being generic, it show competitive results, surpasses highly non-linear models like Autoformer, and being compatative compared a strong base-line which is suited for this task. Results are summarized in the table below, where the number in the headline is the number of steps needed to predict in the future, and the score is the MSE between the prediction and ground truth, lower is better.

| Model        | 96    | 192   | 336   | 720   |
|--------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| Linearizer   | 0.167 | 0.224 | 0.257 | 0.368 |
| PatchTST    | 0.159 | 0.211 | 0.241 | 0.334 |
| Autoformer   | 0.247 | 0.321 | 0.341 | 0.411 |


In summary, in response to the concern, we conducted a broader set of experiments spanning three distinct domains. The results strengthen the empirical evidence that our Linearizer applies robustly to complex and varied tasks. We have added these experiments to the **Applications** section and thank the reviewer for helping us improve significantly the paper’s quality.

[3] Autoformer: Decomposition Transformers with Auto-Correlation for Long-Term Series Forecasting - Haixu Wu, Jiehui Xu, Jianmin Wang, Mingsheng Long.

Dear Reviewer Yo18,

Thank you for the detailed follow-up. We appreciate you clarifying your position and **acknowledging a misunderstanding.** However, we believe that a **misunderstanding persists** regarding the nature of the contribution and its utility.

 

# 1. On the Core Contribution
While we agree to refine the presentation to avoid implying we discovered the concept of "Transport of Structure," we maintain that our contribution is not just a specific architecture diagram. The core contribution is the methodology of deep learnable linearization: **using neural networks to explicitly find and optimize the pair of vector spaces over which a complex target mapping becomes linear while training end-to-end for any task.** While the mathematical existence of such spaces is known (via bijections), the optimization process that simultaneously satisfies a high-dimensional task and enforces the linear basis required for analytic manipulation is a non-trivial machine learning problem. This is the gap our work fills.

 

# 2. On "Triviality"
The reviewer stated that while not all transport of structure is trivial, our specific application is "standard". We struggle to find a consistent metric for this distinction when comparing our work to the fields we cited. Consider Koopman Operator Theory. Its core premise involves linearizing non-linear dynamics in a latent space. Algebraically, this relies on the same fundamental concept of change of basis. Why is Koopman theory considered a non-trivial field rather than a "standard application" of linear algebra?
- It is not because of the equation itself.
- It is because of the development of data-driven algorithms (like DMD and EDMD) that allow us to approximate this theoretical operator from empirical data.

Similarly, consider Kernel Methods. The theoretical existence of a high-dimensional linearizing feature map $\phi(x)$ was well known. The massive contribution of e.g., Schölkopf et al. (1998) was developing the Kernel Trick, a constructive methodology to compute dot products without visiting that space. 

In both cases, the scientific contribution was bridging the gap between the algebraic existence of the operator and its algorithmic realization. Our work performs this function for Deep Learning. The "standard" algebra does not tell you how to parameterize the coordinate map $g$ or the core $A$ to remain invertible, stable, and expressive enough for high-dimensional tasks. We developed the algorithmic realization (the specific architecture and optimization constraints) that bridges that gap, enabling the linearization of complex neural mappings.

 


# 3. On Goals Made Available and Their Linearity
The reviewer claimed that "the induced vector space and its properties are entirely irrelevant for the applications". This is factually wrong. First, we respectfully point out that the reviewer has not addressed our applications (except one) and also disregarded the related claims in our previous response. We re-iterate these applications (to explain why they are not "standard") in the list below and then provide explanation on their crucial dependency on the linear representation of the mapping (to explain why the induced vector space and its properties **are** relevant for the applications).
- A group of works (e.g., Shocher et al., 2024; Durasov et al., 2025; Jensen & Vicary, 2025; Al-Jaff et al., 2025) attempts to enforce **approximate** idempotency on neural networks using sophisticated optimization, when it is in fact possible, as we demonstrate, to have a perfectly idempotent network enforced by architecture, which we then utilize as a novel generative global projector.  
**Linearity:** The idempotency is enforced by making the core operator $A$ a projection matrix, by manipulating its eigenvalues to be binary using a straight-through-estimator. This application relies on the transferability of idempotency between the matrix $A$ and the entire function.
-  We define and calculate a Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverse (Penrose, 1955) of neural networks, a novel and useful element. Our definition maintains the four Penrose identities towards a non-linear neural network. This is used for inversion of generative diffusion models and can be used in many other ways.  
**Linearity:** Without the ability to represent the mapping as a linearizer with its core operator, it wouldn't be possible to calculate the Pseudo-Inverse of the mapping in general. 
- General algebraic tool kit like spectral decomposition, matrix powers, projections, and inversions **of neural networks** are introduced. This has a scientific value, opens doors to future applications and surely relies on linearity of the induced spaces.

Dear Reviewer ojRH,

Thank you for the continued engagement and the precise mathematical feedback. We appreciate you pushing us on these details, as it has helped us significantly refine the rigor of our arguments.


 


1. **On the Lipschitz Correction:** You are absolutely correct regarding the Lipschitz claim. The function $\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]$ is indeed the classic counterexample. We conflated continuity with the Lipschitz property. However, as you noted, Uniform Continuity (which holds for continuous functions on compact domains) is sufficient for the $\epsilon$-approximation argument in Theorem 1. We have corrected this error in the revised manuscript.

 

2. **On Lemma 9 ($ M \le N $):** You are also correct that our specific notation for the linear map construction ($ A^* $) described a projection, which implies $M \le N$. To address this, we have updated the proof in Appendix H to explicitly define $A^*$ for both cases:
    - If $M \le N$: $A^* $ projects onto the first $M$ coordinates.
    - If $M > N$: $A^* $ maps to the first $N$ coordinates and pads the remaining $M-N$ coordinates with zeros (acting as an injective embedding). In both cases, distinct latent points $p_i$ map to distinct targets $q_i$, preserving the validity of the lemma for any dimension.

 

3. **On the Role of the Linear Core ($A$):** We agree with your observation regarding UAP: the non-linear networks $g$ indeed provide the primary representational capacity. As discussed in Section 4.2, the linear operator $A$ is not intended to be a source of non-linear expressivity, but rather to provide specific structural roles, and function as a handle that allows control thus enabling the demonstrated applications:
    - *Rank & Invertibility (General Case):* $A$ determines the rank and null-space of the mapping. If $A=I$ (or is removed), the model becomes a global diffeomorphism (equivalent to a Normalizing Flow), which forces strict invertibility. However, most tasks, such as classification, generation (mapping ambient noise to a lower-dimensional manifold), and projection, are fundamentally non-invertible. $A$ allows us to explicitly model this dimension reduction.
    - *Spectrum (Shared Basis Case):* In settings where $g_x=g_y$ (like Flow Matching), $A$ strictly determines the eigenvalues of the operator, defining the dynamics in the induced space.

 

4. **Utility of $A$ in Applications:** The specific algebraic characteristics of $A$ enable the control required for our applications, which would be impossible with diffeomorphisms alone:
    - *Flow Matching:* We learn a time-dependent operator $A_t$ sharing a fixed basis $g$. The linearity of $A$ is crucial because it allows us to analytically aggregate the steps ($B = \prod M_n$) to collapse the trajectory into One-Step Generation. Naturally, the different linear operators $A_t, B$ have different roles and meanings that cannot be absorbed in $g$. This provides us with a handle to control the mapping with linear tools and eventually collapse the steps to a single one.
    - *Style Transfer:* Similarly, for the style transfer application, we learn a family of operators $A_{style}$ within the same basis. The different styles are represented by different $A_{style}$ while having the same $g_x,g_y$. In this sense $A$ has a crucial role. We even leverage the linear structure to interpolate between styles by interpolating the matrices.
    - *Idempotency:*  By constraining $A$ to be a diagonal projection matrix, we enforce Global Idempotency by architecture. This solves a difficult problem in the literature, where prior methods (e.g., Shocher et al., 2024; Durasov et al., 2025; Jensen & Vicary, 2025; Al-Jaff et al., 2025) struggle to enforce even local idempotency through complex optimization.

 

5. **Clarification on New Experiments:** We interpreted your comment regarding the new experiments ("marginal positive effects") as evaluating them for superiority. We wish to clarify that the goal of these additional experiments (Weather, Disentanglement, Classification) was not to claim SotA superiority over specialized baselines, but to address the specific concern regarding limited expressivity. By demonstrating that the Linearizer converges and matches strong baselines across diverse modalities (Regression, Classification) and topologies, we empirically validate that the architecture is not restricted to specific "cherry-picked" generative niches, but is rather a general-purpose estimator. The new added theorem also aims to show this point exactly. 

 


We thank you again for this discussion, and hope we addressed your concerns. We are happy to keep the discussion going and further improve our paper.

summary.value: This paper develops a methodology for linearizing nonlinear neural networks by applying linear space theory. First, it introduces an algebra (vector operations and a metric) that endows curved spaces with the structure of inner product spaces using invertible neural transformations. Using this, it treats neural networks as linear mappings on curved vector spaces transformed by these invertible networks. As applications, this paper proposes one-step inference via flow-matching, interpolation for style transfer, and the construction of idempotent networks.

strengths.value: Several studies have explored deep learning models that perform linear operations in latent spaces, such as Mixup and state-space models. However, few have provided a theoretical framework for such operations. This paper offers a theoretical framework that reframes neural networks as linear mappings in curved spaces. To my knowledge, no other paper has framed neural networks in this manner.

weaknesses.value:
1. As the authors point out, the proposed linearizable neural networks have limitations in their expressive power. Therefore, I question whether they are theoretically useful architectures.
2. The experiments are limited to generation tasks on relatively small image datasets, such as MNIST and CelebA. Therefore, their significance is limited from the perspective of practical usefulness.
3. I would like more clarification on the benefit of reframing deep learning models as linear mappings in curved spaces. If all neural networks could be interpreted this way, it would be convincing. However, as this paper itself points out, this is not the case. Therefore, it seems more reasonable to view this paper as proposing a specific type of architecture that combines invertible networks with linear mappings.

questions.value: See the Weaknesses section, particularly the third point.

comment.value:
## 3. Empirical Validation: Three new diverse experiments, empirically showing a linearizer converging over various tasks.
While optimizing invertible networks can be challenging, we empirically found that a **Linearizer** can be trained effectively for the tasks we attempted. To address this concern more directly, we broadened our experimental scope with **three** additional and diverse tasks - face attribute classification, disentanglement distillation, and weather prediction - highlighting the robustness of the Linearizer.

**CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA).** We evaluate on the CelebA face attribute classification task, which includes large pose variation, background clutter, diverse identities, and rich annotations (40 binary attributes such as *Male*, *Eyeglasses*, *Blond Hair*). After training, our Linearizer attains a test accuracy of **87.6%**; for reference, a ResNet-50 baseline reaches **86.1%**. These results suggest that the Linearizer handles moderately complex, real-world visual variability.

**Distillation of nonlinear disentanglement models.** Broadening the scope of experimentation, we distill the encoder of a pretrained disentanglement model into a Linearizer (using pretrained checkpoints from [1]). We consider VAE, FactorVAE, and β-VAE on the **dSprites** dataset, which provides ground-truth factors of variation. We assess quality with standard metrics: **FactorVAE**, **SAP**, and **DCI** (disentanglement, completeness, informativeness). Across models, the Linearizer closely matches the original encoders (marked as Linearizer-) on these metrics (see table below), indicating that it can capture highly nonlinear transformations with no loss in disentanglement quality of the encoded representations.

| Model                  | FactorVAE  ↑      | SAP     ↑         | DCI-D    ↑        | DCI-C      ↑      | DCI-I     ↑       |
|------------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| VAE                    | 0.2831±0.0306    | 0.0248±0.0075    | 0.4897±0.0209    | 0.2727±0.0067    | 0.9373±0.0025    |
| Linearizer-VAE         | 0.2875±0.0345    | 0.0232±0.0017    | 0.4945±0.0124    | 0.2704±0.0060    | 0.9348±0.0072    |
| FactorVAE              | 0.3314±0.0135    | 0.0585±0.0086    | 0.6417±0.0120    | 0.5062±0.0051    | 0.9359±0.0035    |
| Linearizer-FactorVAE   | 0.3546±0.0251    | 0.0488±0.0095    | 0.6437±0.0057    | 0.5049±0.0034    | 0.9357±0.0030    |
| BetaH                  | 0.5927±0.0465    | 0.2321±0.0115    | 0.8260±0.0222    | 0.7133±0.0035    | 0.9533±0.0018    |
| Linearizer-BetaH       | 0.6916±0.0496    | 0.2443±0.0083    | 0.7951±0.0038    | 0.7105±0.0038    | 0.9548±0.0010    |



**Weather Prediction.** To further explore the applicability of our framework, we conduct a small experiment in a new domain, regression of future steps. We utilize a standard weather prediction benchmarking, in this benchmark, we need to predict the future, given 96 steps of the past. We compare our method with two well known baselines, the AutoFormer[3] and PatchTST[2], suited specifically for regression task. Briefly, while our method being generic, it show competitive results, surpasses highly non-linear models like Autoformer, and being compatative compared a strong base-line which is suited for this task. Results are summarized in the table below, where the number in the headline is the number of steps needed to predict in the future, and the score is the MSE between the prediction and ground truth, lower is better.

| Model        | 96    | 192   | 336   | 720   |
|--------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| Linearizer   | 0.167 | 0.224 | 0.257 | 0.368 |
| PatchTST    | 0.159 | 0.211 | 0.241 | 0.334 |
| Autoformer   | 0.247 | 0.321 | 0.341 | 0.411 |


In summary, in response to the concern, we conducted a broader set of experiments spanning three distinct domains. The results strengthen the empirical evidence that our Linearizer applies robustly to complex and varied tasks. We have added these experiments to the **Applications** section and thank the reviewer for helping us improve significantly the paper’s quality.

**References**  
[1]  disentangling-vae  - https://github.com/YannDubs/disentangling-vae  
[2] A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers - Yuqi Nie, Nam H. Nguyen, Phanwadee Sinthong, Jayant Kalagnanam.  
[3] Autoformer: Decomposition Transformers with Auto-Correlation for Long-Term Series Forecasting - Haixu Wu, Jiehui Xu, Jianmin Wang, Mingsheng Long.

# What you mean by "space", can it be it a finite or infinite dimensional vector space, an affine space, or a topological space. If can can be an infinite dimensional vector space, what is its topology?

Thank you for this precise question. To clarify:
1. Space: The underlying sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ are finite-dimensional real vector spaces. The field they are over is the field of real numbers, just like the common $\mathbb{R}^N$. They only differ from the base Euclidean spaces in their algebraic structure. Specifically, in the definitions of the two fundamental operations: vector addition ($\oplus_g$) and scalar multiplication ($\odot_g$).
2. Dimension: Our invertible maps $g$ (e.g., $g_x$) are bijections from a space to itself (e.g., $\mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$). Therefore, the induced vector space has the same finite dimension as the original Euclidean space. Our framework is intentionally finite-dimensional. The study of linear operators on infinite-dimensional function spaces to analyze non-linear dynamics is the domain of Koopman operator theory, which we explicitly discuss and differentiate our work from in the Related Work (Sec. 6) .
4. Topology: The reviewer is correct that the topology is critical. Our framework explicitly defines it. We are not using the standard Euclidean topology on $\mathcal{X}$ or $\mathcal{Y}$. Instead, our framework defines a new "Induced Inner Product". We then prove in Lemma 4 that the resulting space $(V, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_g)$ is a Hilbert space. The topology is therefore the norm-induced topology from this new, learned inner product.

 

# Are $g_x$ and $g_y$ and their inverse maps continuous?
This is a subtle issue that is indeed not clear in the main paper. For most of the properties (Lemmas 3, 5, 6, 7) and also for the applications we make no such assumption.  We do point out that neural networks are in most cases continuous. 

However, there are two small subtleties. First, The induced space being Hilbert (Lemma 4) does assume continuity and would not hold without it. Second, the geometric intuition (Sec 2.3) describes $g$ as a diffeomorphism which of course would not be true unless $g$ is continuous and smooth.

We have added a clarification in the revised paper.

 


# When $g_x$ and $g_y$ are represented as neural networks or neural operators, what kind of architecture can you use to ensure that these maps are bijections?
We use additive and affine coupling layers following NICE (Dinh et al., 2015) and RealNVP (Dinh et al., 2017), which ensure bijectivity. The specific architecture and implementation details can be found in Appendix G.

 


# Do you need uniform continuity of the inverses of the maps $g_x$ and $g_y$ to make the $\oplus$ and $\odot$ operations continuous?
First we point out that $\oplus_g, \odot_g$ need not to be continuous for any of the demonstrated applications, and for *almost* all the properties (see continuity question response above).

Now, for $\oplus_g, \odot_g$ to be continuous it is required that $g, g^{-1}$ will be continuous, but not necessarily uniformly.

 


# **On Lemma 3:** Is the function $g_y$ fixed in the space $Y$ when you consider families of functions $X \to Y$?

It depends on what the reviewer means by "fixed".
1. If "fixed" means "Shared" (i.e., shared weights): Then yes. For composition (Lemma 3) to work, the $g_y$ map must be shared between the output of $f_1$ and the input of $f_2$. 
2. If "fixed" means "Frozen" (i.e., not trained): Then no. The entire network is trained end-to-end. This includes $g_x, g_y, A$. All simultaneously optimized within a regular network training procedure of the entire network $g^{-1}_y(Ag_x(\cdot))$ with the regular loss of the desired task.

 


# In formula (14), is the norm the $g$-norm?

Thank you for this truly insightful question. No, the norm in formula 14 is Euclidean. the $g$-norm is a learned norm. Since in general we only train for the regular task objective, allowing the norm to be learned would make a "short-cut" allowing reducing the loss purely by modifying the norm.

I would like to start by thanking the authors for their reply. I will concede that there may be a misunderstanding, but if so, a substantial part of the blame lies in the way the manuscript is written. This is, of course, the only information that I have available. 

Assuming instead that the author's contribution was to introduce a new architecture, the Linearizer, and show that this is somewhat useful in applications. *I agree that this approach would be somewhat reasonable.* But then why spend most of the introduction and the abstract on touting the great theoretical insights? 
The following are just a few examples of the way the importance of the theoretical "insight" is promoted:

- "Is it possible to identify a pair of non-standard
vector spaces for which a conventionally nonlinear function is, in fact, linear?"

- "This framework makes the entire arsenal of linear algebra, including SVD, pseudo-inverse, orthogonal projection and more, applicable to nonlinear mappings."

- "can we reinterpret conventionally nonlinear neural networks as linear operators in disguise?"

- "This perspective not only offers a new lens on neural networks,..."

So the authors do make it appear as if the theoretical insight that one can equip a set with a vector space structure via a bijection was a genuine contribution of their work as well as a major new theoretical insight.

What is more, none of the theoretical results are referred to anywhere in the applications section. Most importantly, the induced vector space and its properties are entirely irrelevant for the applications. For example, the result that multi-step diffusion can be replaced by one step follows immediately from the definition of the linearizer. No vector space needed.
It almost seems as if the vector space structure results are just there to add some sort of appearance of mathematical theory. 

To prevent misunderstandings of their work, *I would suggest that the authors remove the trivial theoretical remarks,* which are well known and demonstrated every semester by countless first-year math students, and focus on what they actually want to demonstrate: That a new architecture performs well on certain tasks. 

I believe the paragraphs above address points 1 and 4 made by the authors.

Concerning point 2:
I find it hard to follow the argument that implies that the fields mentioned by the authors would be rendered trivial. I am sure the authors would agree with me that I have not claimed that every argument that uses transport of structure in some sense is trivial. However, the particular application of the transport structure of this paper is standard. 

Ad point 3: The authors massively oversell their contribution here. If they had, for standard neural network-based diffusion models, identified a way to reduce the number of diffusion steps to one, then this would be a major insight. This has not happened. They introduced a new approach whose main feature is that compositions collapse (note that this requires g_x = g_y and is thus very restrictive!). To illustrate why this is not overly impressive, let's consider the following.

*Def:* We define the Nullifier as the map $N \colon x \mapsto 0$.
If we define a diffusion map as in (13) of the manuscript, then we can compute $\hat{x}_1$ without even applying $N$ once!  I don't even need to look at $x_0$. This is also extremely memory efficient. Surely, no one would be impressed by this! 

Finally, I would like to address the new results briefly. As Reviewers ojRH and TT5Z have already pointed out, there are basic mathematical issues in the new proofs. And as the authors themselves mention, these are really things that are basic: "The function $\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]$ is indeed the classic counterexample. We conflated continuity with the Lipschitz property". The authors confuse compactness with finiteness or different types of continuity. Such mistakes should not happen at a research level.

Dear Reviewer TT5Z,

Thank you for the continued engagement and the sharp mathematical observations. We appreciate you helping us ensure the rigorousness of our theoretical claims.

 


**1. On the Theorem Refinements**
You are correct on both counts, and we have revised the theorem statement in the updated manuscript to be strictly precise:

* **Dimension 1:** Thank you for correcting us on this. Indeed, in $\mathbb{R}^1$, **continuous** invertibility implies strict monotonicity, which prevents arbitrary reordering. We have added the condition $N \geq 2$ to the statement. This aligns with our discussion in **Section 4.1**, where we rely on the degrees of freedom available in the ambient space to resolve topological constraints.
* **Compactness:** Regarding the compactness claim, we agree that our phrasing *"compact set (e.g., a finite dataset)"* was imprecise. While finite sets are technically compact, the phrasing implies validity for continuous compact domains, which our proof does not cover. We have revised the statement to explicitly specify that $X$ is a **finite set** contained within the domain.

 


**2. On "Reframing vs. Architecture" (Your Original Point 3)**
We also wanted to circle back to your 3rd point. Upon reading it again, we believe we understand your meaning better and want to address it directly.

You are correct that our method cannot be used for mechanistic interpretability or as an analytical framework for existing architectures (like NTK is for standard networks). We distinguish between **linearizing existing pretrained architectures** and **using a specific network to linearize a mapping** (input $\to$ output).

Since a mapping can be realized by numerous networks, we offer a framework that realizes this mapping through a *specific architectural choice*. This "linear mapping in curved space" structure is what strictly enables the benefits of using the linear toolkit for complex mappings and tasks. These benefits include collapsing generative sequences into a single step and deriving analytic inverses.

In this sense, our framework does offer analysis, but of the *mapping* itself rather than of the *network* implementing it. On the scientific side, it demonstrates a principle by which we can think of these complex tasks as linear, provided we identify the correct pair of vector spaces.

 


**3. Conclusion**
Finally, since you stated that we partly answered your questions, we would be thankful if you could share any points that were left unanswered. We would be happy to provide further clarifications or add elements that improve the paper.

# "The authors address flow matching as diffusion. As an ODE based method it is not a diffusion process, unlike SDE based DDPM. In a mathematically based paper, such inaccuracies should be avoided."

This remark highlights a subtle and active discussion within the community. While the SDE/ODE distinction is evident, from an algorithmic point of view an equivalence between FM and generative diffusion models can be shown. [Gao et al. (2024), "Diffusion Meets Flow Matching: Two Sides of the Same Coin"](https://diffusionflow.github.io/) explicitly states: "we aim to clear up this confusion and show that diffusion models and Gaussian flow matching are the same" and "you can use the two frameworks interchangeably." However, as the reviewer's comment rightly implies, this equivalence is subtle. For the stochastic case (DDPM), the equivalence to FM is at the distribution level rather than instance level. To avoid confusion and to improve the clarity of the paper, we added a short discussion into the main paper.

We sincerely thank Reviewer ojRH for their deep and constructive engagement with our paper. We are encouraged that they found the core idea "really original" and the contribution "excellent." Their feedback is valuable for improving the clarity and completeness of our work. We address each of their points below:

 

# "The core idea of the paper - looking at vector spaces in non linear coordinates - could be presented somewhat clearer. Many results given in the lemma would then just be clear and in parts superfluous (like Lemma 4). Also all the linear algebra checked in detail would follow from one structural argument."

We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. They are correct that our invertible map $g$ acts as a vector space isomorphism between the standard Euclidean space and our induced space. From this single structural property, most of the linear algebra properties (SVD, transpose, etc.) are indeed straightforward consequences. 

We chose to present these lemmas and their proofs individually in the main text to make the paper self-contained and accessible to the broadest possible machine learning audience and avoid handling reviews that are skeptical regarding the correctness. However, following the reviewer's remark, we added a clarification in the beginning of the properties section regarding this.

 


# "For me the missing part is a detailed investigation of the interaction of the chosen 'coordinate maps' g with the learning task. Obviously not any g would do (e.g. not the identity or linear g's)", "Related to this, I would appreciate a much more extensive analysis of the training details, especially with regard to the previous point.", "Can you give a detailed and reproducible account on how the coordinate maps $g$ are obtained in the respective application context?"

It is true that not any $g$ would do. In fact, only very specific ones that need to be found by optimization. The entire architecture, including the invertible networks $g_x, g_y$ and the linear operator $A$, is trained end-to-end. This optimization is, in effect, learning two things in parallel: the general mapping required by the task, and the optimal coordinate transformation g that allows this general mapping to be linear over the curved space.

All the details for how $g$ is parameterized and learned are in Appendix G (Implementation Details).
- Appendix G.1 (Backbones) specifies that g is composed of 6 invertible blocks.
- Appendix G.1 (Table 1) & G.4 (Conditioners) detail the specific INN architecture (Affine Coupling layers using a tiny U-Net as the conditioner).

Following the comment, we added a concise summary of implementation details in Sec. 2 to clarify the methodology and improve overall readability.  

 



# "Better visualizations would be really helpful for a better representation of the main idea."

Thank you for this excellent suggestion. We have added Fig.10 in Appendix. I that illustrates the geometric intuition for our flow matching application. Our model learns a flow over a geodesic path in the curved $g$-space which are curved lines in the Euclidean space. **We are open to preparing more visualizations according to our further discussion.**

 


# "Also the interaction between the learning task and the expressivity of the linearizers would be of interest. Is the reproduction of the FM time integration with a linear flow compatible with other approaches that do not have as 'stiff' vector fields as FM - take e.g. a likelihood based trained neuralODE. Similar questions arise for the style transfer task."  

Our Flow Matching (FM) implementation is already 'non-stiff' in the sense that it is a curved path in standard Euclidean space. By definition, our path is a geodesic in the induced $g$-space. which maps to a curved trajectory in Euclidean space. Additionally, we have a working variant where the Linearizer predicts the target $x_1$ directly, rather than the velocity $v$, which is the FM practice and experimented with DDIM as well.

# 4. On the "Nullifier" Analogy
The "Nullifier" example ($f(x)=0$) **illustrates the misunderstanding** of the challenge. The reviewer argues that collapsing steps is trivial because a zero-function also collapses steps. However, the Nullifier does not generate images (other than a blank constant result) which is the goal and the main point. The community has invested significant effort into achieving One-Step Generation (e.g., Progressive Distillation, Consistency Models). There is the result and the efficiency. **Result without efficiency is non-ideal; efficiency without result is nothing.**

 

# 5. On Mathematical Rigor
Regarding the corrections to the appendix: The purpose of the peer review process is to identify imprecisions and refine the manuscript. We have acknowledged the oversight regarding 1D monotonicity and the phrasing of compactness, which reviewer TT5Z has constructively commented on. We have rigorously corrected them in the revision and the proof holds. We believe the value of a research paper should be judged by its corrected final state and its scientific contribution.

 

We hope this clarifies why we believe the framework offers a substantial contribution to the field of learnable operators. We are open to further discussion.

summary.value: The paper studies maps that are the composition $g_y^{-1}\circ A\circ g_x:X\to Y$ of an invertible neural network $g_x$, a linear map $A$ and an inverse neural network $g^{-1}_y,$ where the neural networks depend only on the spaces $X$ and $Y$.  In other words, it studies maps from $X$ to $Y$ that can be represented as linear map after the spaces are transformed in a suitable non-linear  way. This makes it possible to bring several tools of linear algebra in a new way to machine learning.  For example  projections, semigroups, singular value decomposition are then formulated for potentially non-linear operators. This is an interesting idea. The paper can be consider also a technically simple way (not in the sense that it is trivial, but easily implementable) to do manifold learning and learn maps between manifolds.

strengths.value: The paper has a clear idea that is well developed. The question when maps or families of maps can be coded or represented as linear maps is simple but the idea is developed in creative and quite deep way. The paper is very well written.

weaknesses.value: The families of the maps which can be represented in the form  $g_y^{-1}\circ A\circ g_x$ may be quite small. In fact, the authors discuss this well and give examples of maps for which their method does not work. However, the authors give also several interesting examples of problems to which they can apply their architecture and this shows that their results are widely applicable.

2. Are $g_x$ and $g_y$ and their inverse maps continuous?

3. When $g_x$ and $g_y$ are represented as neural networks or neural operators, what kind of architecture you can use to ensure that  these maps are bijections?

4. Do you need uniform continuity of the inverses of the maps $g_x$ and $g_y$ to make the $\oplus$ and $\odot$ operations continuous?

5. On Lemma 3: Is the function $g_y$  fixed in the space $Y$ when you consider families of functions $X\to Y$?

6. In formula (14), is the norm the $g$-norm?

7. Do we have any universal approximation results (or approximation results in some restricted class of functions or families of functions) for the linearizers?

8. In general, please explain in more detail what functions in the linearizer are trained. For example if you consider one function from $X$ to $Y$, do you find all the maps $g_x$, $g_y$ and the linear operator
$A$ by training? How training is done when you have a family of functions between the same spaces $X$ and $Y$?

9. In formula (15), what are the properties of  the function $f(x,t)$?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback.
We believe there is a **fundamental misunderstanding** of our contribution, which we would like to clarify. 

 

# 1. Our contribution is making the coordinate change learnable for neural networks, trained end-to-end, and demonstrating key benefits of doing so. We didn't re-invent the math;  we applied it, and this is what the paper describes.
Our paper states repeatedly that our method utilizes a simple **"change of coordinates"**, which, of course, **we do not claim to have invented**. We explicitly note in the proof for Lemma.4 that $g$ is a **vector-space isomorphism** (and a **diffeomorphism**, as noted in our geometric intuition). Furthermore, we emphasise its simplicity in our intuition paragraphs and point to the **pullback metric**. This is to show that we use the existing terms and build upon them rather than claiming to invent anything. This paper makes the change of coordinates **learnable for neural networks**, enforced by architecture so the entire network trains regularly end-to-end, and **demonstrates key benefits** of doing so.

 


# 2. The same measure of triviality, pointed out by the reviewer, would, by extension, render entire fields of science trivial. 
Such as the entire **Koopman operator theory**, including data-driven methods like **DMD/EDMD** (Schmid, 2010; Lusch et al., 2018; Mardt et al., 2018) and all linear bases for dynamical systems in general (Mezić, 2005). Also the **"Kernel trick"** with the  representer theorem and **Kernel-PCA** would be trivial. These all apply transport of structure, each in its own way.


 


# 3. Had it been trivial, the following desired goals, which the review did not address, would have been trivially achieved long ago, yet our work is the first to demonstrate them. 
For example, we demonstrate collapsing diffusion steps to a single, **fully equivalent** one. Further, a group of works (e.g., Shocher et al., 2024; Durasov et al., 2025; Jensen & Vicary, 2025; Al-Jaff et al., 2025) attempts to enforce *approximated* idempotency on neural networks using sophisticated optimization, when it is in fact possible, as we demonstrate, to have a **perfectly** idempotent network enforced by architecture, which we then utilize as a novel generative global projector. We also demonstrate elements like the Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverse (Penrose, 1955) **of neural networks**, including for inverting generative diffusion models.


All of these applications were made possible due to **learning** a change of coordinates **specifically for neural networks** and the observations of what it could be exploited for. As far as we are aware, they are demonstrated by us for the first time. 

 


# 4. We do acknowledge that most of the linear algebra properties (SVD, transpose, etc.) are  straightforward consequences of the vector space isomorphism.
We chose to present these lemmas and their proofs individually in the main text to make the paper self-contained and accessible to the broadest possible machine learning audience and avoid handling reviews that are skeptical regarding the correctness. However, we now added a clarification in the beginning of the properties section regarding this.

 


# While respecting the reviewer's view, we strongly argue that neither the framework nor the applications are trivial.

summary.value: The authors reinvent a classical mathematical technique which I know under the name transport of structure: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_of_structure. This method typically an exercise when vector spaces are introduced.

strengths.value: There are experiments that seem to show some practical value of the approach. The paper is also easy to read.

weaknesses.value:
Theoretically, the whole approach is beyond trivial. Saying that this method is well known would be an understatement of epic proportions. 
This idea is quite literally in every introduction course to linear algebra and functional analysis. It is central in topology,  and geometry. This induced vector space is the whole reason tangent spaces are a thing, hence all of differential geometry is based on it. It is absolutely inconceivable to me that the authors have never come across transport of structure before.

summary.value:
The paper is not ready for submission, as was evidenced by the interactions with multiple reviewers. Reviewers ojRH and TT5Z found (fairly simple) counterexamples to some of the claims, which the authors tried to patch up. As reviewer Yo18 points out---given that the mathematical content of the paper is fairly straightforward and standard, this points to lack of basic proofreading of the paper. As reviewer ojRH also points out, it is unclear the "linearizer" framework does very much by way of the empirical performance---the effect is likely the richness of g_x and g_y, which is supported by prior theoretical results (e.g. Teshima et al). 
Overall, I find neither the theoretical nor empirical contributions merit acceptance.

reviewer_concerns.value: There were numerous errors in the (already very simple) theoretical results, confusing writing and positioning, and lack of discussion on experimental details. I don't believe any of these are adequately addressed in the discussion.

reviewer_scores.value: I do not think the scores of the reviewers would have improved.
